Ecuador Grapples With Sharp Currency Depreciation Amid Financial Turmoil

QUITO, June 14 — Ecuador is facing a mounting financial crisis as the sucre plunged more than 30% against the U.S. dollar over the past two weeks, sparking fears of runaway inflation and deepening economic hardship nationwide. The currency collapse, attributed to dwindling foreign reserves and increased investor uncertainty, has triggered panic buying in supermarkets and a surge in the prices of basic goods.

Economy Minister Lucía Herrera said in a televised address Friday that the government is “taking urgent steps to stabilize the sucre and protect the most vulnerable.” She acknowledged, however, that “the situation remains volatile and difficult for many Ecuadorian families.”

Street protests have erupted in major cities including Guayaquil and Cuenca, with demonstrators demanding government intervention to cap food and fuel prices. The National Confederation of Workers reported that thousands have joined strikes and marches, while union leader Esteban Quinteros warned, “If salaries don’t rise in line with prices, more families will fall into poverty.”

Ecuador’s central bank has raised interest rates to 18% in an attempt to stem capital flight, but analysts at Andean Economic Insight say confidence remains low. “Unless external support is secured, the sucre’s slide may continue,” said economist María Paredes. International organizations have expressed concern; the Inter-American Development Bank said it was “monitoring the situation closely.”

Small business owners report plummeting sales as customers cut spending. “My suppliers now demand payment in dollars, but people have less to spend every day,” said Rosa Medina, a shopkeeper in Quito.

With inflation now running at an estimated annualized rate above 40%, the outlook for Ecuador’s economy remains uncertain as the crisis deepens.
